# Status report: jf2 allocator test on kestrel (2026-11-20)

## Short version

jf2 (our modified jemalloc allocator) reduced 99th-percentile latency by 59% on the read-heavy test. Throughput and median latency showed no difference beyond the variation between runs. The 5.7 GB (9.3%) memory increase still needs approval from the capacity team.

## Words used here

- **kestrel**: our key-value store.
- **jemalloc**: an open-source memory allocator. Build A uses version 5.3.
- **jf2**: our modified copy of jemalloc.
- **YCSB**: a widely used benchmark for key-value stores [Ref1].
- **YCSB-B**: the read-heavy YCSB workload. Its standard mix is 95% reads and 5% updates [Ref1].
- **YCSB-A**: the write-heavy YCSB workload. Its standard mix is 50% reads and 50% updates [Ref1].
- **pN latency**: N% of requests complete within this time. Example: p99 covers 99% of requests.
- **Latency spike**: a short period when requests take much longer than usual.
- **RSS**: resident set size. It is the physical memory that the process holds.
- **kops/s**: thousands of operations per second.
- **us**: microseconds.
- **Decay purge**: jemalloc returns unused memory to the operating system after a delay.
- **perf**: the Linux sampling profiler.
- **NUMA pinning**: binding threads to the CPUs and memory of one socket.
- **logrotate**: a system tool that archives log files. A nightly scheduled job starts it.
- **Staging**: the pre-production environment.

## Goal

Check whether jf2 removes the p99 latency spikes in kestrel.

## Test setup

- **Host**: bench-07 (2 x 32-core Xeon, 512 GB RAM), Linux kernel 6.8.
- **System load**: the load average was 0.4 before the runs (under 1% of the 64 cores).
- **Build A**: commit 4f1c2aa of the main branch, with jemalloc 5.3.
- **Build B**: the same commit, with jf2 in place of jemalloc 5.3.
- **Workload**: YCSB-B with 64 client threads, 10 minutes per run.
- **Runs**: 5 per build, in alternating order (A, B, A, B, and so on).

## Results

Each throughput and latency cell shows the median of 5 runs. The lowest and highest run follow in parentheses. The notes give one RSS value per build.

| Metric | A (jemalloc 5.3) | B (jf2) | Change, B vs A |
|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput, kops/s | 412 (405..418) | 409 (401..415) | -3 (-0.7%) |
| p50 latency, us | 118 (116..121) | 119 (117..121) | +1 (+0.8%) |
| p99 latency, us | 2140 (1890..2610) | 870 (820..940) | -1270 (-59.3%) |
| p99.9 latency, us | 9800 (7200..14100) | 3100 (2700..3900) | -6700 (-68.4%) |
| RSS at end of run, GB | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 (+9.3%) |

In both charts, `o` marks the median. Each `|` marks the lowest or highest run.

```
p99 latency in us (lower is better), one column = 50 us

A                                        |----o--------|  2140
B                  |o-|  870 (-59%)
   +-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+
   0                  1000                2000                3000
```

```
p99.9 latency in us (lower is better), one column = 250 us

A                               |---------o----------------|  9800
B             |o---|  3100 (-68%)
   +-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+
   0                  5000               10000               15000
```

Takeaway: the B range lies fully below the A range in both charts.

### What the data shows

- **p99 latency**: the median fell from 2140 us to 870 us (59% lower). The highest B run (940 us) is below the lowest A run (1890 us).
- **p99.9 latency**: the median fell from 9800 us to 3100 us (68% lower). The highest B run (3900 us) is below the lowest A run (7200 us).
- **Throughput**: the medians differ by 3 kops/s (0.7%). The A and B ranges overlap. So this test shows no throughput difference.
- **p50 latency**: the medians differ by 1 us (0.8%). The A and B ranges overlap.
- **Memory**: RSS at the end of the run rose from 61.2 GB to 66.9 GB. That is 5.7 GB (9.3%) more.
  - Insufficient data: the notes give no range for RSS. Per-run RSS values would show the spread.

### Likely cause of the spikes

- **Measured**: in build A, the spikes occur at the same time as the decay purge. perf attributes 31% of the samples in spike windows to `je_arena_decay` (the jemalloc purge function).
- **Design difference**: jf2 runs the purge in a background thread.
- **Hypothesis**: the latency drop comes from moving the purge to the background thread. A perf profile of build B's slowest periods would confirm or reject this.

### One run was replaced

1. Run 3 of build B stalled for 40 s at minute 7.
2. The stall was traced to the nightly logrotate job, not to the allocator.
3. The run was repeated. The figures above use the repeat, not the original run.

## Not tested

- YCSB-A (write-heavy).
- More than 64 client threads.
- NUMA pinning.

So the results apply only to YCSB-B at 64 threads without NUMA pinning.

## Open question

Is the 5.7 GB (9.3%) RSS increase acceptable? The capacity team must decide.

## Next steps

1. Run YCSB-A tomorrow (2026-11-21).
2. Ask the capacity team to approve the RSS increase.
3. If they approve, enable jf2 in staging, controlled by a configuration flag.

## References

- [Ref1] YCSB core workloads: https://github.com/brianfrankcooper/YCSB/wiki/Core-Workloads

---

Notes for you, not part of the report:

- **Added by me**:
  - the percent changes
  - the two charts
  - the workload mixes from [Ref1]
  - the two flagged gaps (RSS range, build B profile)
- **Assumption**: I read "if ok" as capacity team approval only. If YCSB-A must also pass first, step 3 needs that condition.
